utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'm turning to the Prosecution for the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and the case manager, Kimberly Fleming. Mrs. Fleming, unfortunately, it's the last day with us today, and I wish to thank her for the great work done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant, representing General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant, representing Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to greet everybody in the courtroom who were able to arrive despite the snow that seems to have paralysed everybody, and we can start at the envisaged time. We are very sorry that Mrs. Fleming is leaving the Prosecution, and we appreciate the work that she has done so far in order to allow the efficient presentation of evidence. We would like to thank her for everything that she has done, and we wish her success in her job in the future. Today we have two witnesses on the schedule. They are at the disposal of the Chamber. We shall not waste any more time. We shall bring the first witness into the courtroom, if there are no particular measures to apply for. I'm going to ask the usher to go and bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. First I would like to check whether you can hear my words translated into your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, can. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You have been called by the Prosecution to testify before the International Tribunal. In order to do that, you have to take the solemn declaration. Before that, you will introduce yourself to the Chamber. Can you please stand up. What is your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Zdravko Zulj. I solemn declaration that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Before you read the declaration, you have to tell me where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Zdravko Zulj. I was born in Glavice near Bugojno on the 4th of September, 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a forest technician, and I work in the forestry management company in Glavice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. In 1993, what did you do at the time? What was your profession at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I joined the HVO and I was a member of the HVO at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Have you ever testified in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Now you may read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the procedure is concerned and the way you're going to testify, the Prosecution, on your right-hand side, is going to ask you questions. They will start. When answering their questions, can you please be as precise and as concise as possible. The aim of your testimony is to inform the Trial Chamber of the events that you witnessed. Once the Prosecution has asked you all the questions, then the Defence, seated on your left-hand side, will also ask you questions during their cross-examination. First they need to check whether you are a credible witness and they need to present their case. In addition to that, the Trial Chamber may also ask you questions at any moment, especially when it is necessary to clarify some of your previous answers. Since you have just read the solemn declaration, you have promised to tell the truth. If you give a false testimony, you will be liable for perjury and you may be punishable by a prison sentence up to seven years or a fine. If answering a question you find yourself in a situation that the answer might incriminate you and that your words might be used against you, if you find yourself in such a situation, you may say that you don't want to answer. In that case, the Trial Chamber may compel the witness to answer; however, if the witness has been forced to answer, such words cannot be used against such a witness. I hope you understand. If at any point in time during your testimony you encounter some difficulties, please tell the Chamber so and the Trial Chamber will put the matter right. Having said that, I'm giving the floor to the Prosecution, who is going to start with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj, in response to a question of His Honour, you indicated that in 1992 you were a member of the HVO. When did you join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: On the 4th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon joining the HVO, what were your primary duties or responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: We were on the line between Kupres and Bugojno. That's where we were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was there a different army on the opposite side of the line from where your HVO unit was stationed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, the Serb army. They were in Kupres, and we were in Bugojno on the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there later come a time, Witness, when your HVO unit had involvement with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Later on I joined the military police of the HVO, and that is the time when there were conflicts between the army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall when you joined the military police of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think it was in May 1992 -- no, rather, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in May 1993, when you joined the HVO military police, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: In the Kalin Hotel in the town of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After May 1993, when you joined the HVO, what were your primary responsibilities or duties?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: As a member of the military police, I had to secure some facilities in town. I was involved in patrols together with UNPROFOR around the town. And for a while, we patrolled together with the police of the BH army. However, there were some incidents, and this practice was interrupted. We mainly secured facilities such as Ljubljanksa Banka, the post office, the Croatian hall, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you secured certain facilities. Where are these facilities that you just mentioned located?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Most of them were in the town of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: A few moments ago you mentioned that there were conflicts between the army and the HVO. When you said that, what army were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I was referring to members of the Muslim side. Up to then, there were no conflicts, but there were incidents. People were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did the conflict begin in Bugojno after you were an HVO military policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 19th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which military forces were involved in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: The HVO and the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When this conflict began on 19 July 1993, where were you stationed at that time or where did you report for duty at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I was in the Kalin Hotel at the base of the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you in fact in the Kalin Hotel on the day the war started in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the Kalin Hotel. I arrived the night before. On the 18th of July I reported for duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what was the name or number of the unit, the HVO military police unit, that you were a member of and which was based at the Kalin Hotel in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time the war started on 19 July 1993, do you know how many members of the 2nd Battalion of the HVO military police were in the Hotel Kalin at the time the war started?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think that there were approximately 30 men, not more than that. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the 30 men who were members of the 2nd Battalion of the HVO military police, were there any other people in the Hotel Kalin at the time the war started, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, there may have been the girl who worked at the front desk, maybe a few waiters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After the war started on the 19th of July, 1993, how long did your unit, the 2nd Battalion of the HVO military police, remain in the Hotel Kalin?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Some five or six days, up to the 24th or the 25th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the period between the 19th of July, 1993 and the period of time on the 24th or 25th of July, did any other people come to the Hotel Kalin, other than members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. There is a village in the vicinity of the Kalin Hotel, some kilometre away. It is a Croatian village that had fallen and had been occupied by the Muslim forces. People withdrew, both civilians and members of one unit. I believe that it was a special unit of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that your unit remained in the Hotel Kalin until the 24th or 25th of July. What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: On that day -- I don't know -- on the 24th or on the 25th, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: We were encircled by the BiH army. They were calling to us on the loudspeaker. They wanted us to surrender. They said that there was nowhere for us to go, that we were encircled. And our commanders decided that we would surrender. We left our weapons in the hotel. We raised our arms, and we walked in front of the hotel. In the vicinity of the hotel, there is a parking lot where there is a department store and coffee house. They lined us up there. They searched us to see what we have on us. They took whatever we had of any value, cigarettes, jewellery, watches, and so on. And if anybody had money, they took that away as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following the surrender of your unit, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: We were in the parking lot, and from the parking lot they took us to the basement of the furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were taken with you to the basement of the furniture store?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Some 30 of us from the military police and those people who had joined us from the unit of the civilian police. There were some 20 of them. So all together, there may have been 50 or 60 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where is this furniture store that you've told us about located?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: It is about a kilometre or a kilometre and a half from the hotel, and it is also in the town of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you were taken to the basement of the furniture store. Do you recall approximately what time or what part of the day it was when you arrived in the basement of the furniture store?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I believe that it was sometime in the afternoon, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in the basement of the furniture store, were there people already in that basement?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think that we were the first ones to be taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the conditions in the basement of the furniture store upon your arrival.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: It was dark. The floor was covered with water. There were some pallets on the floor, wooden pallets, that we later on used to sleep on. The water level may have been anything between 5 and 10 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the basement of the furniture store in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think five, six, or maybe seven days. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How were you treated during the time, those five or six or seven days that you were in the basement of the furniture store?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: How? In the evenings, we would be visited by the troops of the army. They took our uniforms and gave us some older uniforms. We didn't get any food until the moment when Sister Pavka came on the second or on the third day. She brought us some tins and breads. As for the hygiene conditions, they were terrible. There was beating. There was ill-treatment. People were taken to the upper floors and they were beaten up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned people taken to the upper floors, where they were beaten. Do you recall the names of any of the individuals who were taken to the upper floors and beaten?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think I do. On the first evening, they took out Stipo Zelic, who was the commander of the military police; also, the commander of the other unit that was with us in the hotel, his name was Cubela. Then they took out Dragan Brecic, Mljenko Bagaric, Zrinko Arazina, Dadic. There were other people as well, but I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As for these beatings, Witness, were you ever personally the victim of such beating in the furniture store?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: On the first day when we were captured, I was asking to go to the toilet. I saw the guard standing. I approached him and I asked him whether I could be allowed to go and relieve myself. He slapped me and he told me that I was supposed to relieve myself where I slept and where I was being accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, while in the basement of the furniture store, where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: On the pallets that were on the basement floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After you remained in the furniture store in Bugojno for five, six, or seven days, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: To the Vojin Paleksic Primary School, to the hall there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, how -- can you tell us the circumstances under which you went to the Vojin Paleksic Primary School?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: They took us there in a lorry, and they drove us to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've made reference to "they"; "they took us there in a lorry." Who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I'm referring to members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were these members of the BH army wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think that most of them had ordinary camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness, whether you knew what unit or units these members of the BH army were from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which units they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you also told us that "they took us to the Vojin Paleksic Primary School." Who were you referring to when you said "us"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I was referring to HVO members, the detainees, and about 20 people or 30 perhaps - I'm not sure - were with me in the first group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate day or month or week and year that you arrived at the Vojin Paleksic Primary School?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I was captured around the 25th of July. I spent five or six days in the furniture showroom, so it may have been at the beginning of August, between the 1st and 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to the group of HVO soldiers that you were with when you arrived at the Vojin Paleksic Primary School in the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: When we got to the school, we got out of the lorry. At the entrance to the hall, BH army members were lined up. As we entered, they'd kick some of us or slap some of us. They lined us up against the wall in the hall. Our backs were facing them. Then there was a burst of fire from an automatic rifle. You couldn't see where they were aiming. You expected to be hit by a bullet, but they probably fired in the air at the ceiling. I think this was to frighten us. But no one was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know which unit or units the BH army members that were at the Vojin Paleksic Primary School were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I don't know the names of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the Vojin Paleksic Primary School?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I don't think I was there for more than ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where is the Vojin Paleksic Primary School located?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: In part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which town?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions in the Vojin Paleksic Primary School for the approximately ten days that you remained there.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, I think they were better than the conditions in the furniture showroom. It wasn't wet and it wasn't dark. At least there was a little light. But as far as the maltreatment is concerned, it was the same. We also didn't receive enough food. I think at one point in time there were 200, 250, perhaps even 300 people in the hall. We'd get 15 to 20 loaves of bread for a meal and a pot of soup without any additives, without any spices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that "as far as the maltreatment is concerned, it was the same." Can you please elaborate upon what you meant by that statement.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I remember that people were also taken out and beaten and maltreated. In the late evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After being in the Vojin Paleksic Primary School, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: To Prusac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber the circumstances under which you went to Prusac.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, they crammed us into some lorries again, perhaps 20 to 30 people. They called us out. We got into the lorry. We got into the back of the lorry, and they drove us away to Prusac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, you said "they called us out." Who did you mean by "they" and who did you mean by "us"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: The soldiers called us out, BH army soldiers. And when I said "we," I was referring to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Prusac?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think we remained there for about three months in total, because earlier on they returned us on one occasion. There was a camp in the Iskra Stadium. They said there was going to be some sort of exchange, so they sent us back and we spent four or five days there, and then they returned the same group to Prusac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, after you returned to Prusac, where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: When I returned to Prusac, we were placed in a house there, which is where we slept. And during the day and early in the morning, we dug trenches and communicating trenches facing the Serbian side. It was at the demarcation line between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After being held in Prusac, Witness, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: They sent us back to the Iskra Stadium again, to the dressing rooms, which is where the majority of the detainees were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The second time you arrived at the Iskra Stadium, do you recall approximately what month or season and what year that was?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think it was autumn 1993, perhaps in October or November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And on this second occasion you were at Iskra Stadium, how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Until the day on which we were exchanged, the 19th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the English transcript says you were released or exchanged on 19 March 1993. Is that the correct date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So just to be clear, Witness, you were exchanged on 19 March 1994 and you were kept in the Iskra Stadium up until that date; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this second period of time that you were at the Iskra Stadium, approximately how many people were detained there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: All in all, because there were some people who would sometimes go to work in Gornji Vakuf or the surrounding villages, in Bugojno, but 300 or 294 or 5. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these people that were detained in the Iskra Stadium soldiers of the HVO, civilians, or both?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think they were mostly HVO soldiers. Perhaps there were a few elderly people, but they were probably members of some sort of a home guard regiment. Home guard regiments had been organised in villages in order to protect the villages. People who were a little older would form them, people who were 50 or 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe the conditions at the Iskra Football Stadium when you first arrived there in October or November 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, they were terrible. I was in a room. It was perhaps 10 by 20. And there were 160 people sleeping in it. The sanitary conditions were non-existent. It was overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the food or drinking water that was provided to you at that stadium.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, at that time, there were some civilians, some Croatian civilians who had remained in Bugojno, and they allowed them to bring us food, which was naturally inspected at the entrance to the prison. Sometimes it was confiscated too. And in particular, if the guards found that they had cigarettes, they would confiscate them. At the time, a pack of cigarettes in Bugojno cost perhaps about 50 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, a few moments ago you described the room, and you said it was 10 by 20. I assume that was 10 by 20 metres?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I think, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the detainees at the Iskra Football Stadium, how were they treated?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, they would also be beaten, taken outside. Sometimes they would let us go out to wash in groups of five or six, but the same things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who would take the detainees out and beat them?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: These people wore masks. And as it was dark, it wasn't possible to recognise them. But I think the guards were involved in that because no one could get in without the guards' permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who were the guards and what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: They were probably members of the BH army. Some of them wore camouflage uniforms and some of them had black uniforms after they had taken them from us. But on the whole, they wore ordinary military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zulj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I'll turn to the Defence now for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Zulj. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and I'm assisted by my two colleagues, Mrs. Edina Residovic and Ms. Muriel Cauvin. We represent General Hadzihasanovic. Following the answers you provided to the questions put to you by the Prosecution, I would like to ask you a number of questions. Some of them are of a general nature and relate to the context in Bugojno, and others are more specific and concern the events that you yourself experienced. First of all, I'd like you to confirm that you met investigators from the OTP on the 13th and 17th of September of the year 2001.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: We met, but I'm not sure of the date, but I think that's the right date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you then provided a statement which you signed. You gave it to the OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on that occasion, you were able to discuss in detail the events that you had experienced in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj, in 1993 you were 27 years old.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You come from the village of Glavice and you had studied in the elementary school -- I apologise, Mr. Zulj. I've been told that your answer hasn't been recorded when I asked you about your age in 1993, when I asked you whether you were 27 years old.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I was born in 1966, so yes, I was 27 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zulj, you did your military service in the JNA in 1985.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your military service in the JNA lasted one year.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Up to the 14th of May, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were a mechanician in an armoured unit.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we go back to the year 1991, you heard about what was happening in Croatia and the inhabitants of your village in Glavice had already established a sort of guard system in order to protect and -- to protect the houses.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in 1992, or more precisely, in April 1992, the Serbian forces attacked Kupres.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In response to the Serbian attack on Kupres, the HVO created the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade consisted of three battalions.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were three battalions within the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There were also some independent units, groups, and other platoons which were separate.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion was created in January 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was the day, the creation of the battalion, the 4th of June, 1992--

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- that you volunteered to join the battalion and you were sent to the front lines in Kupres.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: With the exception of this event in August 1992 when an ambush was laid for you by the Serbian forces, the situation at the front was, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one might say, calm.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: That's correct. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you have told my colleague, you were transferred to the military police at the end of 1992 or at the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in May in 1993. That's when I was transferred to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I stand corrected. Witness, you are quite right. You said May 1993 when answering my colleague's question. But in the statement we have here, it said the end of 1992, beginning of 1993. So I apologise for this error. The military police headquarters was in the Kalin Hotel.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one of your tasks consisted of manning checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also to secure important buildings in the town of Bugojno itself.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As you told my colleague, you were part of a patrol with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in spite of the tension that existed between the HVO and the Muslims, you worked together at that time.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, sometimes we went on joint patrols in the town or with UNPROFOR, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj, can you confirm that in the middle of the year 1992 a number of refugees who had been expelled from Donji Vakuf, Prozor, and other regions arrived in Bugojno and this considerably changed the demographic composition of the town?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this difficult situation resulted in tension between the Muslim and Croat communities, and it also created problems as far as supplies and accommodation were concerned.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. On the whole, it would be something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you also confirm that as of January 1993 there was fighting between the HVO and the army?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, not from January. I think the fighting started on the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj, I'm referring to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, there'd been fighting in Gornji Vakuf before January, perhaps even in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as the conflict between the army and the HVO in Bosnia and Herzegovina increased or increased in Central Bosnia, tension rose in Bugojno too.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: All the inhabitants were afraid that the conflict would spread to the town of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You served within the HVO. You served in the military police. So you are probably familiar with certain events that led or resulted in the conflict that broke out in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: On one occasion, I was assigned the task of escorting a lorry transporting ammunition and weapons. It was supposed to go from Rama to Bugojno. In the village of Gracanica, which is perhaps 6 or 7 kilometres from the town of Bugojno, we, being the military police, went -- drove in a small Lada car and the lorry was behind us. When we passed through Gracanica in that small car, then four or five members of -- I think they were members of the BH army. They came out and took the lorry and drove off in an unknown direction. As a result, they started capturing people. Both sides started doing this. And they started erecting checkpoints. Members of the HVO in Bristovi captured people. BH army members did the same in Vrbanja at the time. I think that Miroslav Talenta was killed in Bugojno and Vucko. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zulj. Correct me if I'm wrong. The event you are referring to at the moment happened in July 1993, a little before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in May there were also certain problems when the HVO captured army members and Emir Jusuf and Sakib Mujkic were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that after these events the BH army captured HVO members and that is when the conflict between the two sides started?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I don't remember that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So these events that happened in May, in your opinion, there were problems before July.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, that's possible, but I can't remember any particular event. But it's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And people worked together in order to avoid a conflict that might break out.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. People continued working and living.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as of July, a number of specific incidents caused the conflict to break out.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: In July?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, in July.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Could you tell me when. Maybe I'll remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To give you an example, Mr. Zulj, the death of your neighbour, Gvozden Stipo.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, that was also at the beginning of July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And after the death of your neighbour, you decided to send your family to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. He was killed. I don't remember the date when he was killed. Because around that time, Vlado Marina was also killed. It was sometime later, on the eve of the conflict. Marina and Talenta died around the same time. And it is true, I sent my family off to Croatia after that happened, when Stipo Gvozden was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was a good decision because a few days later Mr. Talenta was killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He was in Vrbanja at the time. He was on the way back from the swimming pool.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. They went swimming, both him and Vucak, and they were on their way back to the base in Vrbanja and this is where they were killed, in their car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And since you were a military policeman, you probably knew that there was a joint commission that was set up in order to investigate these events.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that. I was just a policeman, an ordinary policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know that sometime later -- did you know that there were Muslim policemen and civilians who were also killed in Vrbanja? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: At that time you mean? No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you know that the HVO had attacked the village of Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: If that had happened, this was during the conflict, after the killing of Talenta, once the conflict spread on a larger scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj, would you then agree with me when I say that the killing of Mr. Talenta triggered -- I'm going to repeat the question, Mr. Zulj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Can you repeat it slowly, because the question was rather complex. Can you please rephrase it, repeat it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zulj, would you agree with me that it was the death of Mr. Talenta, which happened at the beginning of the conflict in Vrbanja -- which led to the conflict, this event that happened in Vrbanja -- and that these incidents in Vrbanja spread towards the town of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. This happened within a day or two after the killing, so yes, a link may be established between the killing and the beginning of this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Zulj, as you have said yourself, the conflict broke out on the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this conflict lasted until the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this date also corresponds with the date when the command of the HVO, which was located in Tito's villa, decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, they didn't surrender. They just left their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At the moment when they left their position, you know that they had set Tito's villa on fire.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: At that time, I was already a prisoner. I heard later on that it had been set on fire. I don't know who did that. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You yourself, Mr. Zulj, on the 18th of July you were at the Kalin Hotel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I was at the burial of Vlado Marina -- either Vlado Marina or Miroslav Talenta. I think it was Miroslav Talenta's funeral. I attended the funeral, and in the evening I reported to the Kalin Hotel for duty. I think it was the funeral of Miroslav Talenta, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when the fighting started on the 19th of July, you were in front of the hotel. You were keeping guard there.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I was in the hotel, yes. We guarded some of the entrances to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during the period of the conflict, you noticed that there were UNPROFOR members who were evacuating people from the Kalin Hotel.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: It was some three or four days after the beginning of the conflict the hospital and the wounded were evacuated, because the war hospital of the HVO was in the basement of the Hotel Kalin and the military police was on the upper floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So on the 24th of July, in the hotel there was nobody. You have already said that there were only 30 military policemen at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. There were some 30 military policemen. There were some 20 members of the civilian police of the special platoon of the civilian police. And there were some 50 or 60 civilians who had arrived from Gaj village to the Kalin Hotel once the village of Gaj had been occupied by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On that day, after the BiH army invited the commander to surrender, your commander decided to surrender, to lay arms.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that time, at that moment, the civilians were separated from the military and civilian policemen from the special unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I believe that we were the first ones to leave the Kalin Hotel. The troops were the first ones to leave the hotel, and the civilians had stayed behind. I don't know what happened to them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that at one moment you learnt that the civilians who had been there were later on taken to the cultural and sports centre.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Some of the civilians later on would bring us food once we -- they were allowed to bring us food, and we would also go to take baths in their houses. They told us that they were first taken for interrogation to the cultural and sports centre and then they were all released. Most of them were released to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you personally, together with other military policemen, were transferred to the furniture store; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: To the basement of the furniture store, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were the first who were put in that place, you who were a group consisting of some 50 men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And those who were in the group were either military or civilian policemen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, the group that was at the hotel. The military and the civilian policemen were taken to the furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as the conflict continued in the town, the people who were in the furniture store were joined by other people.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: On the following day, the 2nd Battalion surrendered and the 3rd Battalion and then the 1st Battalion. So as the battalions surrendered, they would take prisoners and bring them to the furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your stay in the furniture store, it would happen that some of the detainees were called out and taken upstairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in conversation with some of the detainees who had been taken out, you learned that they had been ill-treated. They were -- put bags on their faces before that.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: You could see that when they returned, when they brought them back to the basement. You could see they had been beaten and worked over. And in conversation with them, we learned that they had been beaten. Sometimes they didn't recognise people because either the people who beat them wore masks or they would be put bags on their faces. There was a case when Bajica managed to take the bag off his head and he recognised one of the people who were beating him. And then this person said, "I'm sorry, Barica. I didn't realise it was you who I was beating." So this person knew Barica's first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you personally, while you were in the furniture store, you were never beaten; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I said that on the first day when I asked to go to the toilet I was slapped. I was never taken out and beaten. This never happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I have understood your words well, the words in your statement, while you were in the furniture store you thought that the persons who had been beaten were beaten in order to square some scores.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I suppose that there may have been some old grudges. I heard about Havranek, who had been killed, that he had dated the girl of the person who beat him. These were just rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: A week after you arrived there, you were transferred to the Vojin Paleksic School; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answering to one of the questions, the witness said that he had heard that the person who had been killed, called Havranek, that he had dated the girlfriend of the person who beat him. Can you please explain. What was it exactly that you said about this guy Havranek? What exactly did you say? Can you repeat your question, please -- your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I heard rumours after Havranek's death. And according to the rumour, both Havranek and the guy who beat him dated the same girl. That was before the conflict. So the person who beat Havranek and Havranek apparently dated the same girl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj, let's go back to the Vojin Paleksic School. Before the conflict, this school was the base of the 1st Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your detention in the school, you realised that all those who had previously been detained in the furniture store were in groups in the school.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm going to rephrase it then. During your stay in the school, you realised that all those who had previously been detained in the furniture store were transferred together with you to the Vojin Paleksic School; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I was the one who was in the first group to be transferred to the school. Others arrived later. But I believe that there came a day when we finally ended up all together in the school -- all of us from the furniture store, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I have understood you well, you have mentioned that while you were detained there that you didn't pay too much attention either to the uniforms worn by the guards or their insignia, because you were preoccupied with yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: That's more or less true, but I can say that there were all sorts of uniforms. There were camouflage uniforms, black uniforms. Some guards wore civilian clothes. I didn't notice any insignia. I believe that most of them were the insignia of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zulj. Can you please confirm the following: During that period, a lot of people in Bugojno wore camouflage uniforms or parts of camouflage uniform, both the HVO, as well as the BiH army, even some civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. But it was mostly members of the two armies, the HVO and the BiH army, who wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There were even members of the civilian police who wore camouflage uniforms or parts thereof; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your detention in the school, there was not a lot of food but you, however, received food.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: We received food, but never enough. And the food was of poor quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during that period you were never taken out for any sort of ill-treatment.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, I was never taken out for ill-treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You have answered to my learned friend's question that some persons were taken out during the night and they were ill-treated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you don't know who was it who ill-treated these people.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know their names. But I know that the guards were the ones who called out their names and who took them out. The people who guarded them entered the hall, called out names, and took them out. I don't know who beat them. Even the persons who were beaten don't know who beat them, because they were always masked. Some of them wore uniforms, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj, during your stay in the school, while you were detained there, a lawyer talked to you. There was a secretary with him who took notes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that moment you were asked about your refusal to join the BiH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. The questions were why you didn't join, why a thing like this had to happen, and things along the same line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this interview was correct. It was -- nobody ill-treated you during that conversation.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, nobody ill-treated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, all the detainees were interviewed in a similar manner.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that most of the detainees were interviewed in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during the interviews or after the interviews, a number of the detainees were released.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I believe that the elderly people, those who were over 50 or 60, they were the ones who were released after such interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zulj. In response to my learned friend's question, you talked about the period that you spent in Prusac.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Prusac, yes. Prusac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during that period, would you agree with me that you were never ill-treated there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you. I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, when your names were called out in Prusac, it was always during the night when there was no fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: You mean when they called our names, when ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm going to rephrase my question. If I understood you well, you were taken there to dig some trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. We were told to dig trenches and communicating trenches between the lines that belonged to the army, on the one hand, and the Serbian forces, on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you were digging those trenches during the night, when there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. They would wake us up around 3.00 or 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning, and then -- when it was foggy, and when the fog lifted, they would take us back to have breakfast. After breakfast, they would take us to some secluded places where we would continue digging trenches or dugouts. They would take us to the places where we were not exposed to the enemy fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: None of the people who were with you were either wounded or ...?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, nobody was wounded. Nobody was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And after having spent some 20 days in Prusac, you were transferred to the Iskra Stadium; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. They returned us there and we spent some four or five days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again, you could see that all those who were detained with you in the school were again with you at the Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Most of us. Only those who were taken to do some working, like we were taken to do work in Prusac, were not at the Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you please confirm the following: In your statement given to the Prosecution, you stated that there were toilets at the Iskra Stadium that the detainees could use.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: There was one inside, because -- but it was used rarely, because there was no water, so it couldn't be flushed. And outside there were three or four makeshift toilets that we would normally use either in the morning or during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And after four or five days that you spent at the stadium, you were taken back to Prusac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again, the guards treated you correctly. They gave you food there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you returned to the Iskra Stadium -- of course, you are not sure about the date when you returned; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I believe that it was sometime in the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it could have been the end of October or the beginning of November, maybe.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your detention at the Iskra Stadium, again, food was not good but you did receive food.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, we received food from the Croatian civilians who had stayed behind. They were given permission to bring us food to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when these people brought you food to the stadium, it would happen that the guards confiscated cigarettes; however, the food would be given to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: I said that they would always take cigarettes, but sometimes they would also take food if there was some good tin. And if they found that something that they wanted, they would confiscate that as well. Every time the food was inspected and whatever they wanted to take, they kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zulj, at the Iskra Stadium, there was a routine.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the morning, you were taken out to the outside yard and your names were called out.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, they called our names out every morning. I think they first let us go to wash ourselves. There was a place where there was water. That's where we would go to wash. There was a toilet in the immediate vicinity. We spent an hour there. That's how long it would take all of us to wash ourselves. And then we'd return to the room that we stayed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zulj, some of the detainees at the stadium were sometimes allowed to go home with an escort in order to have a wash or to see their families.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think we all went, but in some sort of order. And people would go in groups of five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Zulj, that at the Iskra Stadium there were also BH army members who were detained there because they were deserters?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: It was divided. We were in one part and they were in another part. But I think that there was a wall separating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zulj, during that period, you told my colleague a while ago about maltreatment that was perpetrated by masked people during the night.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You personally were never singled out for maltreatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you never witnessed these events at night.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, you could mostly -- you could usually hear this. You could hear the groans, especially when we were in the school and in the furniture showroom. But at the stadium, they probably took them somewhere further away so you couldn't hear it. But when people returned, we could see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So in conclusion, Mr. Zulj, during the -- during your period of detention either in the school or the furniture showroom or the stadium, you were not aware of the persons in charge of these centres.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulj, you also know that in Bugojno there were no prisons.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: No, there weren't any, apart from a small one perhaps that was located in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zulj, you would agree with me if I say that since both sides weren't prepared for the conflict, it was necessary to find places where people could be detained?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, if it was necessary to take prisoners, it was also necessary to have a place where these prisoners could be kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with regard to the Iskra Stadium in particular, you also don't know who the person in charge of this stadium was.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Well, there was the guard commander and other people I knew. But I no longer remember the names. I think there was someone called Ceti, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before you met the investigators in September 2001, you met someone called Marijanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you went over certain things with him in order to try to remember the names of the persons you had met in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes. That's a colleague of mine who was detained with me. We live in the same town now. So since we both knew that we would be giving statements in Sarajevo, we met up and spoke about these matters a bit and tried to remember certain names and dates. So we prepared ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And since then, you were exchanged on the 19th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And since that date, you haven't given any statements or you haven't told anyone about the events that you experienced in July and in autumn 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Do you mean in an official way or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, officially, before you met investigators from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO ZULJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zulj. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any questions for the other Defence team? Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: This once again is a witness who's testifying about incident that is Mr. Kubura hasn't been charged with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions on redirect examination, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we are now going to have our Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. break, I would first like to thank the witness for having come to The Hague to testify. You have answered the questions put to you both by the Prosecution and the Defence. We wish you a good trip home. Could the usher escort the witness out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's twenty to 11.00. We will resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now hear our second witness. Has the second witness arrived? That's my first question. And does the Prosecution have any comments to make beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the second witness is available and there will be no application for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Without wasting any more time, the usher will now call the second witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. I would first like to check whether you can hear what I'm saying being interpreted into your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have been called here as a witness, before you start testifying you have to make a solemn declaration. But first of all, I would like to ask you to tell me your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zoran Gvozden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 17th of June, 1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which town?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am an electrotechnician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 or 1993, what was your profession at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before a national or international court, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must now make the solemn declaration. The usher will show you a text that you should read out. You read it out in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Prosecution starts its examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that will be followed. You will have to answer questions put to you by representatives of the Prosecution, who are to your right. They'll ask you some questions which you will answer. To the extent that this is possible, try to answer the questions as fully and precisely as possible. Don't just answer the questions by saying yes or no. We need your answers in order to understand the events of which you were an eyewitness. Once the Prosecution has concluded its examination-in-chief, representatives of the Defence, who are to your left, will conduct their cross-examination and they will ask you some questions in order to check that you are a credible witness and also in order to ask you questions that they consider to be relevant for the defence of the accused. In addition, the three Judges, who are sitting before you, may also ask you questions in order to clarify any matters that might seem to be ambiguous. As you have just made a solemn declaration, you must not lie. And if you provide information that might lead us to believe that your testimony is false, you may be punished. The penalties could consist of a fine or a prison sentence of up to seven years. As you have sworn to tell the truth, we exclude the possibility of false testimony. In the course of the questions put to you, the information you might provide might incriminate you. If that is the case, you can say that you don't want to answer the question. But if the Trial Chamber obliges you to answer the question, the information you provide us with cannot be used to prosecute you at a later date. If necessary, if you encounter any difficulties, inform the Judges of the difficulties you have encountered. If the questions seem to be too complicated or if you don't understand a question, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase the question. Have you understood what I have said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now turn to Mr. Withopf. I think he will be conducting the examination-in-chief. Mr. Withopf, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gvozden.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, you said that you were born in Bugojno. Can you please also inform the Trial Chamber where you grew up.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I grew up in Bugojno too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where did you live in 1992 and in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: In Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you served your military service for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Trial Chamber from when to when.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: From the 5th of September, 1986 until the 5th of September, 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst living in Bugojno in 1992, Mr. Gvozden, did there come a time when you joined the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you still recall a rough date as to when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The official date was the 23rd of May, 1992. That's when I joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And which military unit of the HVO did you join?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I was in the 1st Battalion, the Stjepan Radic Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to which brigade did the Stjepan Radic Battalion belong to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: It belonged to the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where was the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade based?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: In Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, do you recall the 18th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was the day on which I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber how you were taken prisoner and who did take you prisoner.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: On that day, I and three other HVO soldiers went to take up our shift in a village. We had to pass through the town. And we were in a car. We got to the in mosque the centre of town. Members of the BH army came out at that point and took us prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You're making reference to a town you passed through when you were taken prisoner by members of the BiH army. Which town are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: To Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you were taken prisoner by members of the BiH army, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As it was just before the mosque, they put us in a room before -- in front of the mosque where believers washed their feet before they enter the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you were transferred from the area of the mosque to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. About an hour later they transferred us to the grammar school, to the Gimnazija in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And by what means did they transport you to the Gimnazija in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: It was in a military jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you arrived in the Gimnazija in the centre of the town, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: They took us to a room before the Gimnazija, and that's where we remained until evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where were you taken to in the evening?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: In the evening, we were taken to the basement in the Gimnazija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please, Mr. Gvozden, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber describe the basement of the Gimnazija.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The basement in the Gimnazija dated back to the days of Austro-Hungary, and in the basement it was very low and there were three rooms. We were put in the middle room, which was fairly low. At the front it was about 2 metres high, and at the back, a metre and a half or a metre 40 centimetres, and it was about 3 metres wide and 5 or 6 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was there a window in the cell you were just describing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there weren't any windows in the room that we were in because it was right under the front entrance to the Gimnazija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How many of you were detained in the basement of the Gimnazija school?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: On that evening, there were ten of us. And then in the course of the following days, they would bring in another four or five persons. So in the end, there were up to about 45 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were these 45 people in the one cell you just described?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe the living conditions for the 45 people in this one cell.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The conditions were terrible. It was the end of July. It was very hot and humid, and the room was small. There were a lot of people in it. They only let us go to the toilet on a number of occasions, but we had to relieve ourselves in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were you able to lie down?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No. We were only able to sit in a cramped position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long were the 45 people detained in this one cell?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: About two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how did you manage to sleep, if at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, sitting in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the food conditions in the cell.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: When we arrived there, when we were in that room before the facility, we got a tin of fish and some bread. Later they gave us mouldy bread, a little bread for a lot of us, and then something that I couldn't even call soup. It was just warm water with a few beans or something like that, a little rice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were you guarded whilst you were detained in that cell?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: There were guards there, but not down where we were but at the exit. In the hall on the floor, they were always up there, but there were bars and this was always locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who were the guards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: BH army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity, Mr. Gvozden, of the people detained in the basement of the Gimnazija building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were they all Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were they civilians, soldiers, and/or soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were only a few people who were civilians, in my opinion. All the others were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
