utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I would like to use the Sanction technology to show the witness a prior Prosecution exhibit; namely, Prosecution Exhibit P58.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, on the screen in front of you, you see a building. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what this building is about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: That is the Gimnazija building in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the building in whose basement you were detained?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the transcript, the witness Gvozden identifies the building on the photograph Prosecution Exhibit P58 as the Gimnazija school building in which he was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long were you personally detained in the cell?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: For about two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the course of these two weeks, did you become aware of any beatings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber who was beaten.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: 13/1:18 Franjo Jezidzic, Vinko Ivkovic, Mario Subasic and Gordan Rajic were beaten. They were beaten the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: They were beaten the most. Does this mean that others were beaten as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Not to the same extent, but sometimes someone would be slapped, but that was nothing in comparison to the beatings that the others were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber in more detail about the beatings Franjo Jezidzic, Vinko Ivkovic, Mario Subasic, and Gordan Rajic suffered.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, they would come and take them up and send them back covered in blood. They were so weak that we had to make some room for them in that very small room so that they could get a little rest after these beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: They were covered in blood once taken back. Can you please describe in some more detail the injuries they had as a result of the beatings.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Gordan Rajic was beaten with I don't know what, and I believe that his left shoulder was fractured from the beating. The beating was so heavy that his whole shoulder was split.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And Franjo Jezidzic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: He was also heavily beaten, but I can't say how heavily. He was bleeding. He was all black and blue. He was physically and psychologically tortured. He was in a very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying earlier on, Mr. Gvozden, that the four individuals you detailed were taken out. Who actually took them out for the beatings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: One of the guards would call their names and then they had to go upstairs on their own. One man would always come downstairs, call the people's name, unlock the cell door, and let the men go upstairs, walk upstairs on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You are saying that guards took the victims out for the beating. Who actually brought them back into the cell?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Again, somebody would always accompany those persons to unlock the cell and let the men go in, because we ourselves couldn't leave the cells unless somebody unlocked it for us. And usually this lad who was there who would lock and unlock the door -- he was from Donji Vakuf, I believe. But I believe also that he was mentally handicapped, that he was a bit retarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the somebody who brought the victims of the beatings back, was this somebody a guard as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: What do you mean whether he was a guard or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying that guards took the victims out for the beatings. And the question is: Did guards bring the victims back?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. This lad was always there, either on the staircase or in the corridor. He was the one who brought us water. So there was this lad who was always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, what's your blood type?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: O-negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did the fact that your blood type is O-negative, did this fact at some time you were detained in the Gimnazija school building play a role?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, in Gimnazija -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber for what reason it played a role.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: One day a man appeared on the staircase and he asked for at least two or three volunteers with the 0-negative blood type.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did somebody volunteer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And after nobody had volunteered, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Then they called out my name and the name of another man with the same blood type. They knew what our blood types were because when we were captured, they took away our military booklets from us and our blood types were indicated in our military booklets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once your name and the name of the other man was called out, what did happen then? What did happen then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: They took us to the hall of that building, and there I found a commander of the Kuljanski Sejtan BiH army unit. His name was Sabic 13/9:25 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did this Sabic do with you and the other men?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: There was a military policeman there together with Sabic. His name was Cetin. They told us we would be taken to the hospital to give blood was apparently Cetin's brother had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This military policeman with the name Cetin, which army did he form part of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber whether you were taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. The two of us were taken to the hospital very soon after that, and then they took us to the basement because the conflict between Croats and Muslims was still going on at the time. In the meantime, a nurse was not there, so we had to wait, and Sabic said that he was going to inspect some of his unit members who had been wounded as well. We stayed alone with Cetin. The nurse appeared very soon after that. Then they asked me if I had ever had jaundice or any other infectious disease. I had -- I said no, I didn't. And the other guy who was with me - his name was Lucic - he said that he had had jaundice a few years back, so they said that they wouldn't take blood from him but only from me. And it seems that they needed a lot of blood, so they took a double dose from me. As far as I know, 300 grams would constitute a single unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This hospital in which your blood was taken, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: It is located some 100 or 150 metres away from the Gimnazija building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After your blood was taken, were you brought back to the Gimnazija building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, Cetin took us back to the Gimnazija building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And for how long afterwards were you detained in the Gimnazija building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Five or six days, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After these five or six days, were you brought to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. One day they came to fetch us. They returned us to this room in front of the Gimnazija building where they kept us on the first day, and then they transferred us to the sports hall of the Gimnazija building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And from the sports hall of the Gimnazija building, did they transfer you to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: In the sports hall, there were people from the 2nd Battalion of the HVO. On that same day, they put us in cooler trucks, all of us who had been in the basement. And they took us to a part of the town where there is a building that they originally wanted to put us in, but there was no room. So they had to take us to the furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know the building they originally wanted you to put in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. It is a building that belonged to nuns. Later on it was the Marxist Centre. They brought us behind that building. We were in the cooler truck, but once the cooler truck stopped they opened the door. They probably wanted to put us in that building. But since there was no room, they closed the door and they drove us to the furniture store.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this building that belonged to nuns, is it also known as the convent building in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a convent before the Second World War. The building belonged to the nuns, but it was confiscated during the Communist reign and the Communists turned it into a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who brought you from the sports hall of the Gimnazija school building via the convent building in Bugojno to the furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Members of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What's the distance, to your knowledge, Mr. Gvozden, between the Gimnazija school building and the convent building, the convent building and the Slavonija Furniture Salon, the Slavonija Furniture Salon and the Gimnazija school building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: From the Gimnazija to the convent, the distance is about 200 to 250 metres. Between that building and the furniture store, there may be 300 metres approximately. And the distance between the furniture store and the Gimnazija is also a couple hundred metres. Basically we're talking about a triangle formed by these three buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the furniture salon in Bugojno, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: They took us behind the furniture store and they told us to go to the basement of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And you're making reference to "they told us to go to the basement of that building." Who are the people you are referring to as "they"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Members of the BiH army who brought us there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please, Mr. Gvozden, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, describe the basement in the Slavonija Furniture Salon.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: There were about 10 or 15 centimetres of water on the floor, and people found some pieces of furniture in the basement. They broke it apart, put it on the floor so that they could use the boards, the wooden boards to sleep on. It was very dark. There was no light at all. There were no windows because the whole basement is under the ground level. There were only a few oil lamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your recollection, what was the size of this basement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I don't know, maybe 20 metres long and 10 or 12 metres wide. That is as much as I could tell in that darkness that we were put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, I wish to show the witness two photographs. These are again Prosecution exhibits used earlier on; first Prosecution Exhibit P65.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on the photograph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: This is the furniture salon shown from the other side, depicting the main entrance into the store.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the building in whose basement you were detained?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Gvozden, are you saying that this photograph shows the building from the other side?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Because this is the main entrance to the furniture store. In the back, there was another side entrance that probably served to bring the goods in and served as the entrance to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And which entrance was used when you were brought to the furniture salon?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The back-side entrance, in the back of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the transcript, the witness Gvozden identifies the building shown on the photograph Prosecution Exhibit P65 as the Slavonija Furniture Salon he was detained in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, I'm now going to show you, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, another photograph. It will again appear on the screen in front of you. This is Prosecution Exhibit P66. Mr. Gvozden, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: This is the basement in the furniture store building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the basement in the furniture salon in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, it is. This is exactly what it looked like. It had these columns, like I see them in this photo. So yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gvozden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, for the transcript, the witness identifies the room shown on the photograph Prosecution Exhibit P66 as the cell in the basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon he was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long have you been detained, Mr. Gvozden, in this room?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Approximately two weeks, the same amount of time I spent in Gimnazija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how many people in addition to you were detained in this room?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Between 120 and 150, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And for how long, to your knowledge, were these between 120 and 150 people detained in this room?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, some were brought immediately after the fall of Bugojno, which means that they had been there for two weeks prior to my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: We were there for two weeks, and then we were all transferred to the Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber how the detainees managed to sleep in this room, if at all.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I've already told you. There was some furniture there. People put pieces of the furniture on the floor, and there were also glass bottles, some 25 centimetres high that used to contain saline infusion, and we used those bottles to sleep on them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the basement of the Slavonija Furniture Salon, Mr. Gvozden, did you become aware of any beatings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. It happened at the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what did happen at the beginning of August?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: One evening -- actually, it was around 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning -- we could hear voices above us, Brecic, Kosak were called out, but not both of them at once. It was first Dragan Brecic whose name was called, and he had to go out and go upstairs. We could hear blunt noises of him being hit, and then he started screaming. This lasted for maybe five or ten minutes. Then he was returned down the stairs to the basement and the other name was then called. Franc Kosak was called next, and he fared the same as Dragan. Then another person was called. Five names were called altogether, but I can't remember the other three names. And this third person was returned to the basement very quickly as well. After that, Mladen Havranek was called to go out. Again, we heard his screams and we could hear him saying, "What have I ever done to you? Why are you doing this to me?" Some five or ten minutes later he was returned. He managed to negotiate the stairs on his own with great difficulty. And when he came downstairs, he fell first on his knees and then sideways on the floor. A few of us approached him and carried him to his place, or shall I call it his bed. He was still conscious and all he kept saying was, "What have I ever done to them?" Very soon he stopped talking. We thought that he fainted, but that was not the case. We couldn't feel his pulse or anything. We couldn't feel his heartbeats. We wrapped him in a blanket. We started carrying him towards the gate, and we started shouting so that the guys who were upstairs could hear us. We shouted, "What have you done? You have killed this man."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you here for a second, Mr. Gvozden. You Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. just said that "we couldn't feel his pulse or anything. We couldn't feel his heartbeats." Were you amongst the people who tried to feel -- unsuccessfully tried to feel his pulse and his heartbeat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. There was another person who I believe was a paramedic by profession, and he was also a basketball coach in Bugojno. He tried to do something, but we couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What happened after you were shouting upstairs, "What have you done? You have killed this man"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: These people who were upstairs, they scattered. Only one guard remained who heard us. He told us to bring him upstairs and leave him there and then for us to go back downstairs to the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did you do so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We went back down. We left him up there. And later we only heard someone arrive in a car. But we asked in the meantime that guard allow us to go to the toilet at least, as the toilet was upstairs. So we stood in the middle of that flight of stairs. We saw the ambulance taking him away, and perhaps ten minutes later either that same vehicle arrived or perhaps another ambulance. And then they took the other four persons away, the other four persons who had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber who had called out for the beatings the victims Dragan Brecic, Franc Kosak, and Mladen Havranek?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Members of the BH army called them out. The young guard who was up there, I didn't know him personally but I knew him by sight. As far as I know, when Donji Vakuf was liberated, he died. He was killed. His appearance was quite remarkable. He was tall, fair. He had long hair that he wore in a pony-tail. He himself said when this event happened to Mladen, he said, "Why was this necessary?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Gvozden, when you became aware of the objects used for the beatings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, when we went to the toilet that morning in that upper area behind the flight of stairs, in fact, behind the wall there were a few bars, metal bars and wooden sticks. And there was blood on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the size of the metal bars and the wooden sticks.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The bars were 70 or 80 centimetres perhaps, and the wooden sticks were perhaps a metre and a half to 2 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how thick were they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: 5 times 8 centimetres. That was the size of the wooden ones. And the metal bars -- well, I don't know exactly, but they resembled the metal feet that a military bed has.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you still have a recollection, Mr. Gvozden, even if it's only a rough one, as to the date Mladen Havranek died?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I think it was on the 6th or the 7th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Earlier on, Mr. Gvozden, you mentioned that there were about 120 to 150 detainees in the basement of the furniture salon. What was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Up to 150. They were all Croats. Perhaps there were a few Serbs, but they were either HVO members or -- as far as I know, there weren't any civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Gvozden, when you were transferred to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: After Mladen's death, they transferred all of us to the Iskra Stadium in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who did transfer you to the Iskra Stadium in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The BH army military police and their soldiers did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How far is the Iskra Stadium away from the Slavonija Furniture Salon?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, about 500 metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What happened to you, Mr. Gvozden, and the others who were transferred to the Iskra Stadium once you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: We were placed in a big room under the stands. There weren't any windows but only bars, metal bars covered with nylon, a nylon sheet. And that's where we were detained, in that big room, although there were smaller rooms. But we weren't detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the Iskra Stadium together with the other detainees from the Slavonija Furniture Salon, did there come a time when other people had to join you as detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the 1st Battalion arrived later. Up until then, they'd been in the Vojin Paleksic Primary School. People who had been in the Gimnazija were brought in. They took our place there. And as far as I know, there were some other people who were in the town or in the flats and houses. They were subsequently brought there. And I think that some people who had remained in the police basement in the MUP were also brought in. So almost all the detainees were in fact in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what's the number of detainee we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, a total of about 300, but not at all times because quite a few people went to carry out work. As far as I know, 60 people went to Gornji Vakuf. They actually spent two months up there. So the number was never complete in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the about 300 detainees, were they all soldiers or were there also civilians amongst them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, perhaps there were a few civilians. All the others were HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether the Iskra Stadium was secured, and if so, by what means.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: At the beginning, we were only locked up. There was a door at the entrance to the stands. Each cell had its own door. And at the beginning, when we went out in the morning for our names to be called out, after our names had been called out, we could walk around a bit outside. And since there was a small river in the vicinity, we could wash ourselves there because there wasn't any water inside. But later they made a metal fence closer to the stands and we were no longer able to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection, Mr. Gvozden, as to when this metal fence was made?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: In September/October of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The year is 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was it possible, Mr. Gvozden, to your knowledge, to enter the premises of the FC Iskra Stadium without permission of the people who guarded the FC Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No. They didn't even allow our people to come from the other side of the river, not even close to the fence. There was a house where they had some guards, and this was a sort of reception area. If someone appeared and wanted to bring us something to eat, they had to go to see them first and then they would perhaps grant permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with your permission, I wish again to show the witness a photograph which has been used earlier on in this proceedings. It's Prosecution Exhibit P62.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you can see on the photograph in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I can see the Iskra Stadium in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the Iskra Stadium you were detained in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, for the transcript, the witness has identified the building on the photograph Prosecution Exhibit P62 as the FC Iskra Stadium he was detained in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, were there people who guarded the Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, they were members of the BH army. There were at least three of them on each shift and sometimes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber describe the daily routine in the Iskra Stadium.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, at 7.00 every morning we had to go outside, and then one of the guards or the camp warden, as they called him, read out the names of the detainees from a list. Everyone had to respond. We then had to spend about 10 or 15 minutes outside. And we'd prepare -- or set some water aside the day before to be able to brush our teeth and so on. And then we could walk around for 10 or 15 minutes perhaps, and then we were taken back inside. And it was only at lunchtime at 2.00, half past 2.00 or 3.00 they would let us go outside again to have something to eat. And then we were returned to our cells again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just mentioning that the Iskra Stadium was guarded by ABiH soldiers. Are you actually able or were you actually able to identify to which unit these ABiH soldiers which were the guards at the FC Iskra Stadium belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, most of them were members of the military police. They had the military police and brigade police, but in general they had the same insignia. They called them the brigade police. But this wasn't the case for all of them. Some just had uniforms or they had patches that belonged to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The brigade police you are referring to, which brigade is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The 307th Motorised Brigade that was part of the BH army. That's what they called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were mentioning earlier on, Mr. Gvozden, that people were taken out for quite substantial periods of time, I recall you said two months, to Gornji Vakuf. To your knowledge, what had these people to do in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The people in Gornji Vakuf, as far as I know and according to what they told me later, were digging a tunnel beneath the demarcation line in Gornji Vakuf and they would also dig trenches and communicating trenches in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did all people who were digging trenches in the area of Gornji Vakuf, did they all come back to the Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No. Two persons were killed and 10 or 12 of them were wounded. Jezidzic Dragan was killed and Zelko Tabakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how did you get to know that these two people were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: We found out about this only when all the others returned from up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what did you find out from the others about the circumstances they were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: They said they had been hit by a sniper. That's all I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were you yourself, Mr. Gvozden, also taken out to do work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. But I always went in the direction of Donji Vakuf and to the area where there was a demarcation line between the Serbs and the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what was -- what were you made to do at the demarcation line between the Serbs and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Whenever we went up there, we either dug trenches or made dugouts for them. Or we dug out potatoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The trenches you were made to dig out, were they close to the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The trenches weren't that close to the demarcation line, but they were in a very visible spot because there are fields where we worked and an open area facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did there come a time whilst you were digging out trenches at the demarcation line against the Serbs that the Serbs actually shot at you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, when we were filling in a small dugout, they opened fire. A sniper started shooting at us. I assume it was a sniper because there were -- their trenches were quite far away. They opened fire again, but the BH army soldier said that in spite of what was happening we had to continue working. He sent us back there, and he took shelter behind a big tree. He stood by the tree and he said, "If you don't want me to kill you, let him kill you." And then the Serbian sniper probably noticed. As they say in our country, he got it. He realised that we were detainees. He shot at the guard a couple of times and that was it. He then took us back. We didn't remain there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long were you and the others being taken out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, I'd spent 10 or 12 days at the most doing that. Sometimes three days or six days, ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were you then brought back to the Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, whenever there was a new shift, then they would return us to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who returned you to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The BH army soldiers returned us there. It depended on the unit that was present at the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Coming back to the Iskra Stadium. Did there come a time that to your knowledge the Red Cross visited the Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. The Red Cross appeared in September 1993, and I think that they returned a few months later. On that occasion, they just gave us some forms that we had to fill in ourselves. They said that we had been registered by the Red Cross and that we were safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Mr. Gvozden, when you became aware of any plans to be transferred to somewhere else from the Iskra Stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, they brought three big lorries. One man appeared who took a list of 150 persons. He read from the list. And when the first lorry was full, they covered it with its tarpaulin. They started filling the second lorry. It was half full. I was there and there were two or three men behind me. Their commander then appeared - the military police commander, Dautovic - and he said that everything was being postponed until the following day. And we were supposedly supposed to be taken to the KP Dom, the penal and correctional facility in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And do you have a recollection, Mr. Gvozden, as to when this happened, in which month?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: In 1993, October or November, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long were you detained in the Iskra Stadium, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: From the 18th of July until the 18th of April, 1994. Until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm asking about the Iskra Stadium only.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: From the beginning, the first half of August 1993, until April 1993 -- or, in fact, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what happened in April 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: There was an exchange on the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how was the exchange organised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, the day before, they told us that there would be an exchange the following day. And nine Red Cross lorries appeared on the following day and members of the international forces were present. And representatives of the International Red Cross and of the BH army read through a list. People entered the lorries, got into the lorries. When the people got into the lorries, they covered them with tarpaulins and then we set off in the direction of Gornji Vakuf towards the territory where HVO members were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where did the actual exchange take place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: In front of the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In front of what stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The Iskra Stadium in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how many detainees from the Iskra Stadium in Bugojno were exchanged, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In preparation of the exchange, were you made to do something?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. On that first day, we were told that we had to shave so that we'd be clean-shaven on the following day. Only one man who hadn't shaved since 1974, they didn't force him to shave. But everyone else had to shave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were detained in the Iskra Stadium, did you keep any notes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I had a little notebook, and I took notes about the people who were with us, about where we were, about how long we had been there. But a few days before the exchange, a BH army soldier appeared. I didn't know him. And he asked me to give him the notebook. He said it would be best if I did so. I gave it to him. I didn't see him again. He just took the notebook and left. I don't know how he found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gvozden.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for the time being I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's half past 12.00. We'll have our usual break and we will resume at five to 1.00 for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are not getting any translation. Obviously there's nobody in the booth, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gvozden, my name is Stephane Bourgon. I'm accompanied by Mrs. Residovic and Ms. Muriel Cauvin. We represent General Hadzihasanovic. You have answered the questions put to you by my colleagues. I have a few questions for you, both of a general and of a specific nature, questions that concern the events of which you were a witness in 1993. First of all, Mr. Gvozden, in the year 2001 - in April, to be more precise - did you meet investigators from the OTP and did you give them a statement on that occasion which you signed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On that occasion, Mr. Gvozden, you discussed in detail the events that happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If the information I have is correct, in 1993 you were 26, you were born in Bugojno, and you went to the school in Subotica, which is where you lived in 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your military service in the JNA was between 1986 and 1987, and you were in the navy at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you left, about a year later you held the rank of a soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you joined the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade, it was on the 23rd of May, 1992, in order to serve in the 1st Battalion, which was created on that very day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This brigade, as you know -- or rather, could you confirm that this brigade was created in response to the aggression of the Serbian forces against the town of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you also confirm that this brigade consisted of three battalions, a number of independent units, and also some groups and platoons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your battalion - you were a member of the 1st Battalion - was called the Stjepan Radic Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your battalion was deployed in the area of Kupres. It was deployed on the front lines facing the Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gvozden. I'll now move on to the context of the conflict in 1993. In 1992, Mr. Gvozden, the relations between the Muslims and the Croats, if I'm not mistaken, were good. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the two communities cooperated in order to defend the town of Bugojno against the Serbian aggression?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, but not at the very beginning, because the HVO held the entire line in Bugojno. It was only later that the BH army took over the defence in the direction of Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Gvozden, when the Muslim forces weren't yet established, the HVO occupied the entire line, both in Gornji Vakuf and in Kupres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was only later, after the BH army had been established, that the HVO continued to occupy the line in Kupres; whereas the line in Donji Vakuf was transferred --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Donji Vakuf. I apologise. That line was handed over to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And in 1992, you know that the town of Jajce fell into Serbian hands and the Muslim population was expelled towards Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Not towards Bugojno. Towards Travnik. But the people from Jajce, from Travnik came to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gvozden, are you aware of the fact that following this event refugees arrived in droves from Donji Vakuf and Prozor and from other regions? They came to Bugojno. They arrived in Bugojno, and this had a significant effect on the demographic composition of the town of Bugojno. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There were also many Croats among these refugees, but they passed through Bugojno in order to establish themselves further away near the coast.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This increase in the number of population in Bugojno created tension between the various communities and also created problems concerning supplies and accommodation. Do you agree with me about this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, in principle. But the conflicts were not only due to the influx of Muslims. It was also due to the fact that there had been previous conflicts in Vares, Kiseljak, Novi Travnik, Stari Travnik, in Uskoplje. So in all the neighbours towns, there had already been conflicts between the two peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, I myself was going to say the same thing, based on the information that I have. The news from Vares, Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, with regard to the conflicts Muslims and Croats reached Bugojno and contributed to the tensions increasing between Muslims and Croats in Bugojno. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Since you were a member of the HVO during 1993, you certainly know about the incidents that led to the outbreak of conflicts between Muslims and Croats in Bugojno itself in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I know some things. I know that some things did happen. I know that there were sporadic shootings between members of the HVO and the BiH army, but this was all based on individual discords, discords between individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gvozden. Do you know that the HVO in May 1993 captured members of the army of BiH and that Emir Jusuf and Sakib Mujkic were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know in that same period in May the BiH army captured 20 members of the HVO and that from that moment on a conflict started between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Believe me, I didn't know that. I know that there were sporadic arrests and exchanges, but people would be arrested in the morning and released in the afternoon. So these were all rumours circulating around the town and nobody paid too much attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: However, you know, Mr. Gvozden, that all the sides cooperated in order to prevent the conflict spreading to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You also know that there was an incident on the 17th of July in Vrbanja village when Talenta was killed. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, Talenta and Vucak were killed. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And since these two individuals were killed, do you know that there was a mixed Croat-Muslim commission that was supposed to investigate the circumstances of their death?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation, to see whether the interpretation is completed. I apologise. Mr. Gvozden, your answer has not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, when this commission went to Vrbanja, you know that three Muslim policemen were killed on that occasion and that their bodies were thrown into the river.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And after that event or those events, rather, or because of these events, on the following day the HVO attacked Vrbanja and the village was destroyed. 54 soldiers were killed and 45 civilians were made prisoners in the Kalin Hotel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: What date did you mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 17 July.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: 17 July?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the eve of the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: This happened before the conflicts broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because of these incidents in Vrbanja, there was a conflict -- actually, the conflict spread to the town of Bugojno; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the conflict between the BiH army and the HVO started on the 18th or maybe 19th of July in the morning.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: It was either between the 17th and the 18th or the 18th and 19th. I was already detained. I was already in Gimnazija, so I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about the details of what was going on outside at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I totally agree with you, Mr. Gvozden; however, you do know that this conflict lasted up to the 26th of July, the day when the HVO staff, which was located in Tito's villa, decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, they just withdrew. They didn't surrender. None of them surrendered, as far as I know. They just withdrew. They just abandoned that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At the moment when they abandoned that place, they set it on fire.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that it had been set on fire. I don't know who did that, because I don't know. Maybe it would make sense if you are abandoning a place to set documents on fire or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gvozden. Of course, don't hesitate to say that you don't know if you don't know an answer to one of my questions. On the 18th of July, you personally, together with three other members of the HVO, were on the road to Crnice and members of the BiH army stopped you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Among those soldiers, there were persons in uniform and others in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You surrendered your weapons and then they took you to a mosque; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: They took us to a mosque, in a room in front of the mosque, not to the mosque itself, as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: After this incident, four other Croats were taken prisoner and brought to the same place.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: There were four of us and then six other persons were brought in one by one. There were ten of us. We were then taken to this area in the Gimnazija and then two soldiers joined us. And before we were finally put in the basement of the Gimnazija, the two last persons who joined us were exchanged on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gvozden. During the period from the moment when you were arrested and the moment you were transferred to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Gimnazija, you were treated well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we were treated well. And I didn't have any complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you arrived, they put us in the courtyard or in the sports hall in the Gimnazija.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: It was an area that was surrounded by the sports hall and the Gimnazija. That's where we spent the entire afternoon up to the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you arrived, you received both food and water.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: We received a tuna tin from the humanitarian aid, and we also got some bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, at the moment when you arrived in the Gimnazija, in the evening you were transferred to the basement, you could hear what was going on outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: We didn't hear anything. Just a few sporadic shots. Nothing else. We couldn't hear anything else because it was one day before the conflict actually started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the course of the following days, you realised that the conflict was getting more intense.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was shelling and there was more intense fire. There were shots on the Gimnazija as well. You could hear shots in the town. The Gimnazija is in the centre of the town, and yes, we could hear rifle fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you know that the HVO was in the Kalin Hotel? You knew that? And also in the cinema hall, and that the shots came from there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: You know what? What tell you shots came from. I couldn't see. I was only inside. I wasn't outside. I can't tell you where shots came from. Most probably this is where the shots came from. Those were the two points held by the HVO close to the Gimnazija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You were also in the position to realise that the BiH army deployed a number of troops there because of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of troops in the Gimnazija. I don't know how many, but there was a relatively large number of them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you could also hear screams and shouts of people who were tense, and from -- based on all that, you could conclude that war had started.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: The guards told us that the conflict had started, yes. And then they would occasionally come. At that moment, we could not know what was the truth and what wasn't. They told us this place had fallen, the other place had fallen, we had captured this or that. They were just giving us information, and we could take the information at its face value. That's all we could do. We didn't have any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as the conflict went on, as the time passed, you realised that there were more people who joined us in the cells.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Correct me if I am wrong, but it seems to me that you have said to the investigator of the OTP that there were four cells but that at the beginning only one was full.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: There were not four cells but three. The three cells in a row. As you go downstairs, there is one cell straight in front of you and two on each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the basement in that cell where you were, it was hot but still you were given water.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, but not as much as we needed. It was really terribly hot. It was very hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In response to a question by my learned friend, you testified that there were toilets that you could use.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Only when we were allowed to use them, because these toilets were upstairs in the corridor. Downstairs there was no water or anything else, so we couldn't use the toilets as much as we wanted to. Only when we were allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Gvozden, during the period while you were detained in the Gimnazija, you were not ill-treated.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You have also testified that several people's names were called out to go out.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, several people's names were called out. Their names were called out one by one, and then they would be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also, that people who were in the basement were hit and slapped.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You also mentioned to the investigators of the OTP that during your detention, that the detainees could not communicate because the guards were close.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We did talk, but we did not volunteer any comments about the conflict or any such thing, because everybody was concerned about what would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the people whose names were called out, they were not randomly chosen. There was a system.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I don't know what the system was, why certain people's names were called. But every time a name was called, the name would be called from the upstairs. The lad who was in charge of opening the cell would open the cell and that person had to go out. How they selected people, I don't know. Were there any old grudges involved in that or something else? I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the person who opened the cell door and who took the detainees out and brought them back, that was always the same person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As far as I know. This lad was from Donji Vakuf, and he was just an errand boy, just a stooge. And as far as we could all seeing he was a bit retarded. He did not do us any harm. He was quite benevolent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At one moment, Mr. Gvozden, a person came and asked whether there are any detainees with a -- O-negative blood.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: He didn't come downstairs. He was standing on the top of the stairs and he asked for volunteers who had that blood group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then you were told that blood was needed for a wounded person who was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: They had taken our military booklets when we were first arrested. Not at the moment of the arrest. That's when they only took our weapons. When we arrived in the Gimnazija, they took all of our belongings. I had a wallet. I had a Swiss pocket knife. They took that away from me. They didn't touch my money or anything; they just took my military booklet away. And in that military booklet, I myself put my blood type, and that's how they knew that I had the same type. At least, that was my case. I don't know what was the case with that other lad who had the same blood type. It was only when we went upstairs that the military policeman told us that his brother had been wounded and that he needed the blood for his brother. And that's when they took us to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Since nobody volunteered, they called your name and the name of Niko Lucic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you were informed that the blood was needed for the brother of the guy called Cetin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You probably know, Mr. Gvozden, that your blood type is very specific.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Those who have O-negative blood group are universal donors.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, they are universal donors but they can only receive their own blood type.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You were then taken to the hospital, where a normal medical procedure was applied to give blood.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No, it was not a normal procedure. I'm not saying that I would not have given blood, but they took two dosages, two amountfuls of blood. It would have been humanitarian on my part to give just one dose, but to take two doses from me, under those conditions, in the light of the food that I had received up to then, I don't think that was very humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: However, you are happy that you've been able to save this person's life.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I know the man personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as for this other person, Lucic, he had had jaundice and he didn't give blood.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he had had jaundice a few years back and he said, "If you don't believe me, go into my file in the hospital and you will see for yourself." So they didn't take blood from him because they found the record of his previous illness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to the information that I have, he was even given medicines at the time to treat him.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know or did you know that the blood that you gave was intended for Cetin's brother?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So this was a special case.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, yes, this was a special case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This gentleman, Cetin, told you that Mr. Sabic whom you also saw -- that he was a very dangerous person.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: When we were being taken there, he said that he expected us to try and escape on the way to the hospital and that for that reason we shouldn't be tied or anything. This Sabic was well known as an arrogant person. He used to be a policeman before the war. And as far as I know, we all had very bad experiences with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: However, you also mentioned that Mr. Sabic was the commander of the Kuljanski Sejtan unit. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to my information, this used to be Mr. Baclija Sipo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that this Sabic was the commander, or maybe he was the deputy commander. In any case, he was always there in the old school where the base of this unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to my information, Mr. Cetin was not a member of the military police but became a member of the military police in 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe that he was a military policeman even before that. On that very day, he was in uniform. It was ten years ago, so I really can't remember any -- all the detail. I can't remember whether he had insignia or not. But it did happen that a lot of people did not have any insignia at all, no patches whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I absolutely appreciate that, Mr. Gvozden. In July you were put in a refrigerator lorry and transferred from the Gimnazija.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And first you were transported to the convent.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Up to the back-side of the convent, opened the door. The guards came out of the convent and said that the convent was full and that we should be taken somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the lorry started searching for another place and then you arrived in the furniture store.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On your arrival at the furniture store, you were put in the basement.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There were already 100 people or so there when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: There were between 80 and 100. It was very dark. There was very little light, so one couldn't really tell with any precision how many people there were. But I believe that there were between 80 and 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, a little while ago my learned friend showed you the photograph of the basement in the furniture store. You recognised the columns in the basement.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I said that this room, this basement -- I knew this basement from before the war. This used to serve as a showroom for kitchen units, and I knew this area and I remember those columns and I remember that they were there before the war. And when they brought us there on that day, it was daylight and we knew where we were. Bear in mind that we all grew up in the area. We were familiar with a lot of places there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the photo that you were shown, I believe that you will agree with me the photograph depicted just one part of the basement where you were detained.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The basement was much larger, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: I told you that it was 12 metres by 20 metres. That is approximate side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And there were some wooden pallets there. There were some furniture. And there were those bottles that you described, that you used to sleep on them in order to avoid water that was on the floor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The people who were in charge of the furniture salon --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would kindly ask to go into private session, because I have to mention the name of the person who was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, as far as the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the light of the difficulties with the supplies in Bugojno and the fact that the detainees could not be fed regularly, the civilians were allowed to come to the furniture salon and bring food to you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, from time to time. It very much depended on the guard and on their mood. It was all very, very individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your mother was allowed to bring food.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, the little that she had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during your stay in the furniture store, you personally were not ill-treated.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You were also telling us about a night during which about five names were called and these people were ill-treated on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Those who were ill-treated during that night told you that they put plastic bags on their heads so they wouldn't be able to see those who beat them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the event concerning Mr. Havranek very briefly. When he returned to the basement and you took care of him, you realised that he was in a very bad state.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in response to a question from my colleague, you said that you covered Mr. Havranek and you went up crying out that they had killed a man.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. We put a blanket over him and took him to that flight of stairs. The four of us carried him there, and we just wanted to get him up there. We wanted to try to help him, but we weren't able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you went up, there weren't any guards there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No. We got halfway there, because in the meantime this first person, Mr. Barnjak, was being treated by them. And when we got halfway there, we just saw this guard. I mentioned him before, the young man whom I know by sight. He's from Prusica. It's a village near Donji Vakuf. He was fair and had a pony-tail and he said, "Wait." And perhaps it took a second or two, a minute at the most. We just heard some footsteps. A few people went out. And then he let us take him up and he said, "Put him down on the ground and go back."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you saw Mr. Barnjak up on the floor, he said that the people who were beating him, that they had just gone out.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: He was sitting by the wall of the -- by the stairs, and he still had a bag over his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And following this event, you noted when you went to the toilet that an ambulance had had arrived to take Mr. Havranek away.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We remained there, and we told this guard to let us go to the toilet because if there are 120 or 150 people, you'd expect someone to be up there at all times. And through the open door, we could see the ambulance. They put the late Havranek in the ambulance. And then about 15 or 20 minutes later they left because the hospital was only about 100 metres away. They came back then and they said that the four persons who had been beaten should go with them. They were taken to the hospital and they must have been provided with medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, after this event relating to Havranek, the conditions in the furniture showroom improved.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, they improved in that there were no more beatings. They were more liberal. They behaved more liberally towards us when they brought in food and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And while you were detained in the furniture showroom, you were taken to the sports and culture centre for an interview with a judge from the municipal court.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on that occasion, you weren't maltreated in any way.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you didn't mention to this judge at the municipal court the event. You didn't tell him what had happened with Havranek in the basement.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No. In fact, I'm not sure whether I went there before Havranek died or afterwards. I don't know when I went to see the judge, before or after. But I said that on that morning, when all that happened, a young man called Bakir - he was 16 or 17 years old and he was a guard there - he approached me. I didn't know him. And he said he would take me to the parish office to see the priest so I could ask him if he could help us in any way, give us toilet paper or oil or food. And I said, "Well, how am I to go there, given what has happened?" He said, "Don't worry. Just go with me." He took me there. I saw the priest. I told him what had happened. I told him about Havranek and about the fact that these four men had been taken away and I asked him to try and find out what had happened to them, to find out whether they were in the hospital or whether something else has happened to them. He said that he would try to contact the international forces and others. And finally, they found out that they were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then at that moment you took all the things that the priest gave you to the furniture showroom.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, he gave me a litre of oil and some toilet paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, you never knew who was in charge of the furniture showroom.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And since you were worried about your fate as a detainee, you didn't pay any attention to the insignia that the guards wore. And according to what you have told the representatives of the OTP, none of them had any particular signs on them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, there were very few military policemen in the BH army who had full uniforms and white belts and military police insignia, a white patch on their arms. Usually they had a coat after arms with lilies. Most of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during this period in Bugojno, Mr. Gvozden, there were a few people who wore uniforms or parts of uniforms. There were the HVO members, the army members, there were civilians, and there was the civilian police too.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, you were transferred to the Iskra Stadium, which had just been transferred into a prison.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first half of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you have told us about your arrival there. You have described the routine, the roll-call in the morning, the fact that you were able to wash, and the meals you had in the afternoon. You have spoken about all of this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozden, you were personally asked to carry out work on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Gvozden, I am told that your answer to my last question hasn't been entered into the transcript. So my question was: Following the description of your routine in the Iskra Stadium - that is to say, the roll-call in the morning, the fact that you were able to wash, and the fact that there were meals in the afternoon - you can confirm all of this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll interrupt you at this moment. You said meals in the afternoon. Where did you get this from? We were under the impression that meals were distributed in the course of the afternoon. Perhaps the witness could add something or explain this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, about 2.00 or 3.00, that's when it usually happened. There wasn't a set time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have almost finished with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You told representatives of the OTP that when you were carrying out work there were no risks, since both sides were very well aware of what was happening and that people had been asked to carry out this work.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Well, it was dangerous, but it all depended on which BH army members were with us. Some just wanted to maltreat us psychologically because when I worked up there, perhaps I hadn't had a shave for 60 or 70 days. And on that occasion, there were five of us. We all had 20-centimetre-long beards. And the guard who was with us said, "Whoever turns up unshaven in the morning shouldn't turn up. He'll be killed." But he wasn't there in the morning; someone else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But in general, the guards always treated you well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: On the whole, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you mentioned the events in Gornji Vakuf a while ago and people who were transported there to dig trenches, et cetera, it was a situation that was dangerous and fire was opened.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This isn't something that you personally experienced.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: They fared far worse than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This event was something very different from your experience when you were summoned to carry out work.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you were at the Iskra Stadium, you were not maltreated.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you have said that the maltreatment depended on the guards who were there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you remember a guard called Salkic, a football player.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Salkic guard said -- told anyone who wanted to approach the detainees that he would die before they could approach the detainees. Do you remember Salkic saying this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. That happened one evening while we were at the stadium. He was on guard. He was one of the guards. And you could hear a lot of noise outside, a few people appeared. You could hear some voices. I don't know how many people there were. They asked for someone. And Salkic said for as long as he was there, for as long as he was alive, they wouldn't be allowed to enter. And then these quarreled and these people left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say, Mr. Gvozden, that the guards at the stadium all wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN GVOZDEN
utterances.text: Yes. There were civilian police jackets, camouflage jackets, or just trousers. But on the whole, they were all soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
